$$ Q^{0}(x):=\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}\omega_{0}\,\nu(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}b_{j}^{(1)}\nu_{-j}(x). $$

Recall from Lemma A.11 that $\nu_{j}(x)$ is a linear function

$$ \nu_{j}(x)=\frac{\delta_{j}(x_{j}^{\star}-x)}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}. $$

Thus $\nu(x)$ is a degree $s$ polynomial and $\nu_{-j}(x)$ is a degree $s-1$ polynomial for all $j$ (A.14). Hence $P^{0}$ is an $s+1$ degree polynomial with leading coefficient

$$ \mathfrak{p}:=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}(-1)^{s}\prod_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}\neq 0. $$

Similarly, $Q^{0}$ is a degree $s$ polynomial with the same leading coefficient $\mathfrak{p}$ . Thus if we define $P=P^{0}/\mathfrak{p}$ and $Q=Q^{0}/\mathfrak{p}$ then

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}=\frac{Q^{0}}{P^{0}}=\frac{Q}{P} $$

and $P,Q$ are both monic polynomials. Finally, we need to prove that $P$ or equivalently $P^{0}$ has $s+1$ distinct, non-zero real roots that are not in $\overline{\mathcal{S}_{c}}$ . Recall from the definition of $\nu_{j}$ that $\nu_{j}(x_{j}^{\star})=0$ and $\nu_{j}(x)<0\iff x>x_{j}^{\star}$ . Recall from Lemma A.12 that $\{x_{1}^{\star},\dots,x^{\star}_{s}\}$ are all distinct and larger than all numbers in $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ . Assume without loss of generality that $x_{1}^{\star}<x_{2}^{\star}<\dots<x_{s}^{\star}$ . Recall from Remark A.13 that $\nu_{-i}(x_{j}^{\star})=0$ for all $i\neq j$ . Thus, by definition of $P^{0}$ we have

$$ P^{0}(x_{i}^{\star})=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x_{i}^{\star}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x_{i}^{\star}). $$

This means that $P^{0}(x_{i}^{\star})$ has the same sign as $(-1)^{i-1}$ since

$$ \nu_{1}(x_{i}^{\star}),\dots,\nu_{i-1}(x_{i}^{\star})<0<\nu_{i+1}(x_{i}^{\star}),\dots,\nu_{s}(x_{i}^{\star}). $$

Thus, the sequence $P^{0}(x_{1}^{\star}),P^{0}(x_{2}^{\star}),\dots,P^{0}(x_{s}^{\star})$ alternates sign, so by the intermediate value theorem there is a root $\gamma_{i}$ of $P^{0}$ such that $x_{i}^{\star}<\gamma_{i}<x_{i+1}^{\star}$ . This gives us $s-1$ real roots and $\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{s-1}\notin\overline{\mathcal{S}_{c}}$ . Next, note that $\lim_{x\to\infty}P^{0}(x)=(-1)^{s}\infty$ and since $P^{0}(x_{s}^{\star})$ has the sign of $(-1)^{s-1}$ there exists another root $\gamma_{s}>x_{s}^{\star}$ , and thus $\gamma_{s}\notin\overline{\mathcal{S}_{c}}$ . Since $P^{0}$ is a degree $s+1$ polynomial, and we found $s$ real roots, we conclude that $P^{0}$ has indeed $s+1$ real roots. Let the other root be $\gamma_{0}$ such that $P^{0}(x)=\mathfrak{p}(x-\gamma_{0})\dots(x-\gamma_{s})$ . By Vieta’s formulae,

$$ P^{0}(0)=c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\nu(0)=\mathfrak{p}(-1)^{s+1}\prod_{j=0}^{s}\gamma_{j}=-\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\prod_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}\prod_{j=0}^{s}\gamma_{j}. $$

Since $\nu_{j}(0)>0$ for all $j$ , we deduce that all terms in $P^{0}(0)$ are positive, hence $P^{0}(0)>0$ . Since $\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{s}$ are all positive, we deduce that $\gamma_{0}<0$ and hence $\gamma_{0}\notin\overline{\mathcal{S}_{c}}$ . The proof is now complete. ∎

### D.3 Proof of Lemma D.2

#### Proof.

We choose the numbers $\gamma_{k},t_{k}$ inductively over $k\leq d$ such that

$$ \mathfrak{g}(\gamma_{k})=t_{k}\gamma_{k}^{d-k}(\gamma_{k}-\gamma_{k-1})\dots(\gamma_{k}-\gamma_{0})+t_{k-1}\gamma_{k}^{d-k+1}(\gamma_{k}-\gamma_{k-2})\dots(\gamma_{k}-\gamma_{0})+\dots+t_{0}\gamma_{k}^{d} $$

and such that (D.2) is satisfied. The base case $k=-1$ (no pairs chosen) is trivial. Next, assume we have chosen $\gamma_{0},\dots,\gamma_{k}$ and $t_{0},\dots,t_{k}$ for some $-1\leq k\leq d-1$ such that (D.2) and (D.4) are satisfied for all $0\leq j\leq k$ . Consider the following polynomial:

$$ \displaystyle R_{k}(x) \displaystyle:=\mathfrak{g}(x)-\Big[t_{0}x^{d}+t_{1}x^{d-1}(x-\gamma_{0})+\dots+t_{k}x^{d-k}(x-\gamma_{0})\dots(x-\gamma_{k-1})\Big] \displaystyle\hskip 130.0002pt+(t_{0}+\dots+t_{k}-\mathfrak{q}+1)x^{d-k-1}(x-\gamma_{0})\dots(x-\gamma_{k}). $$

where for $k=-1$ the bracket term is empty. Note that the bracket term has degree at most $d$ , and so does the last term. Since $\deg\mathfrak{g}\leq d$ , we deduce that $\deg R_{k}\leq d$ . Moreover, we immediately deduce that the coefficient of $x^{d}$ in $R_{k}$ is

$$ \mathfrak{q}-(t_{0}+\dots+t_{k})+(t_{0}+\dots+t_{k}-\mathfrak{q}+1)=1. $$

This means that $\deg R_{k}=d$ hence $R_{k}$ has at most $d$ real roots. Note that by the base case of induction, equation (D.4) yields that $R_{k}$ vanishes at $\gamma_{0},\dots,\gamma_{k}$ . Since $M$ has $d+1$ elements, we can choose $\gamma_{k+1}\neq 0$ that was not chosen before such that $R_{k}(\gamma_{k+1})\neq 0$ . Finally, let

$$ t_{k+1}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}(\gamma_{k+1})-\Big[t_{k}\gamma_{k+1}^{d-k}(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{k-1})\dots(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{0})+\dots+t_{1}\gamma_{k+1}^{d-1}(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{0})+t_{0}\gamma_{k+1}^{d}\Big]}{\gamma_{k+1}^{d-k-1}(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{k})\dots(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{0})}, $$

which is well-defined since the roots $\gamma_{0},\dots,\gamma_{k+1}$ are distinct and non-zero. Multiplying both sides of this equality by the denominator yields equation (D.4) for $\gamma_{k+1}$ . Note that

$$ \displaystyle R_{k}(\gamma_{k+1}) \displaystyle=\mathfrak{g}(\gamma_{k+1})-\Big[t_{0}\gamma_{k+1}^{d}+t_{1}\gamma_{k+1}^{d-1}(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{0})+\dots+t_{k}\gamma_{k+1}^{d-k}(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{0})\dots(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{k-1})\Big] \displaystyle\hskip 130.0002pt+(t_{0}+\dots+t_{k}-\mathfrak{q}+1)\gamma_{k+1}^{d-k-1}(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{0})\dots(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{k}) \displaystyle=t_{k+1}\gamma_{k+1}^{d-k-1}(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{k})\dots(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{0})+(t_{0}+\dots+t_{k}-\mathfrak{q}+1)\gamma_{k+1}^{d-k-1}(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{0})\dots(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{k}) \displaystyle=(t_{0}+\dots+t_{k}+t_{k+1}-\mathfrak{q}+1)\gamma_{k+1}^{d-k-1}(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{0})\dots(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{k}). $$

Since $R_{k}(\gamma_{k+1})\neq 0$ , we deduce that $t_{0}+t_{1}+\dots+t_{k+1}\neq\mathfrak{q}-1$ and the induction step is complete. We claim that this is a valid choice of coefficients. Consider the polynomial

$$ \mathfrak{g}(x)-\big[t_{d}(x-\gamma_{d-1})\cdots(x-\gamma_{0})+t_{d-1}x(x-\gamma_{d-2})\cdots(x-\gamma_{0})+\cdots+t_{0}x^{d}\big], $$

which has degree at most $d$ since $\deg\mathfrak{g}\leq d$ . By the construction, equation D.4 yields that this polynomial vanishes at $\gamma_{0},\dots,\gamma_{d}$ . We conclude that it must be the 0 polynomial, hence equation D.1 holds. Finally, by construction, equation (D.2) is satisfied so the proof is complete. ∎

## Appendix E Necessity of $s$ Distillation Steps - Proof of Theorem 3.4(b)

### E.1 Proof of Theorem 3.4(b)

We construct a family of examples where $s$ -step SD is actually required to achieve the optimal shrinkage function $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ , and thus proving Theorem 3.4(b). Recall polynomials $P,Q$ from Lemma D.1. First, we provide a purely algebraic condition on $P$ and $Q$ that guarantees that $s$ is the smallest number of distillation steps at which the optimum is achieved.

#### Lemma E.1.

Recall $P,Q$ from Lemma D.1. If $P$ and $Q$ are coprime, i.e. do not share a root, then $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ can not be achieved by $(s-k)$ -step self-distillation procedure for any $1\leq k\leq s$ .

From Lemma B.2, we know that $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ solves a fixed point equation:

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)=g(x)-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\langle f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}},h_{j}\rangle_{w}\,h_{j}(x). $$

Let $A_{j}:=\langle f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}},h_{j}\rangle_{w}$ . Using the definitions of $g,\{h_{j}\}_{j}$ we have:

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)=\dfrac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\mu_{j}(x)}{w(x)}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}A_{j}\mu_{j}(x)}{w(x)}=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\mu_{j}(x)\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}(1-A_{j})}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)}. $$

For simplicity, we assume that $\sigma_{0}=1$ which is without loss of generality by scaling. In the following, we will fix any choice of parameters $r,c,\omega_{0},\dots,\omega_{s}$ and fix $\delta_{1},\dots,\delta_{s}>\max\{\sqrt{c},2c\}$ . The latter assumption that all spikes are above the BBP phase transition is to simplify the exposition and is not crucial. We first establish an uniform, a priori bound.

#### Lemma E.2.

For any choice of parameters $r,c,\omega_{0},\dots,\omega_{s},\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}$ and $\delta_{1},\dots,\delta_{s}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}(1-A_{j})^{2}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}. $$

In particular, we deduce that $1-A_{j}$ are all bounded uniformly. This is also true as $\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\to\infty$ , so by Bolzano-Weierstrass applied $s$ times we can choose a sequence $\{\sigma_{k}^{2}\}_{k=1}^{\infty}$ that diverges to $\infty$ such that for all $j\in[s]$

$$ A_{j}^{\sigma_{i}}\xrightarrow{i\to\infty}A_{j}^{\infty}<\infty, $$

where $\{A_{1}^{\sigma},A_{2}^{\sigma},\dots,A_{s}^{\sigma}\}$ are the coefficients obtained for $\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}=\sigma^{2}$ , keeping all the other parameters fixed. It is clear that $|1-A_{j}^{\infty}|$ are uniformly bounded for all $j$ .

Next, we need to introduce the following notation. Let

$$ P_{i}(x):=P_{\sigma^{2}_{i}}(x)=x\left(\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x)\right)+c\,\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{r^{2}}\nu(x), $$

$$ Q_{i}(x):=Q_{\sigma^{2}_{i}}(x)=\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\omega_{j}(1-A_{j}^{\sigma_{i}})\nu_{-j}(x), $$

$$ Q_{\infty}(x)=\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\omega_{j}(1-A_{j}^{\infty})\nu_{-j}(x). $$

Note that by the same argument as in Lemma D.1, $P_{i},Q_{i}$ and $Q_{\infty}$ are real polynomials with $\deg P_{i}=s+1$ and $\deg Q_{i}=\deg Q_{\infty}=s$ . In the following, we will work under the assumption that $\delta_{k}|1-A_{k}^{\sigma_{i}}|<1/2$ for all $k\in[s]$ and all large enough $i$ . The following results present an example of parameters when this inequality holds.

#### Lemma E.3.

For all $\sigma_{i}^{2}$ large enough, we have $\delta_{k}|1-A_{k}^{\sigma_{i}}|<1/2$ for all $k\in[s]$ .

Next, let us summarize the idea of the proof. Note that if all real roots $z$ of $Q_{i}$ are at constant (uniform in $i$ ) positive distance from $x_{1}^{\star},\dots,x_{s}^{\star}$ and do not escape to $\infty$ as $\sigma\to\infty$ , then $\nu(z)\neq 0$ , so we can make $\sigma^{2}$ large enough to make the numerator non-zero. That is $P_{i}$ and $Q_{i}$ cannot share a root. We make this rigorous via the next two lemmas.

#### Lemma E.4.

Assume $\delta_{k}|1-A_{k}^{\sigma_{i}}|<1/2$ for all $k\in[s]$ and $i\geq 0$ . Then there exists $\varepsilon>0$ and $N_{\varepsilon}$ such that for all $i\geq N_{\varepsilon}$ , all real roots $z$ of $Q_{i}$ satisfy

$$ \min_{j\in[s]}|z-x_{j}^{\star}|>\eta_{\varepsilon}, $$

where $\eta_{\varepsilon}>0$ is a positive constant that depends on $\varepsilon$ , i.e. for all $i$ large enough the roots of $Q_{i}$ are at positive distance of the roots of $\nu(x)$ .

The second claim is that roots of $Q_{i}$ do not escape to $\infty$ .

#### Lemma E.5.

Assume $\delta_{k}|1-A_{k}^{\sigma_{i}}|<1/2$ for all $k\in[s]$ and $i\geq 0$ . Let $\varepsilon$ and $N_{\varepsilon}$ from Lemma E.4. Then, there exists a constant $M$ that does not depend on $i$ such that $|z|\leq M$ for all real roots of $Q_{i}$ with $i\geq N_{\varepsilon}$ .

Using these, we conclude the section with the proof of Theorem 3.4(b).

#### Proof of Theorem 3.4(b).

We claim that there exists $\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}$ such that $P$ and $Q$ do not share a root. Choose $\varepsilon,\eta_{\varepsilon},N_{\varepsilon}$ from Lemma E.4 and $M$ from Lemma E.5. Since $\nu$ vanishes only on $\{x_{k}^{\star}\}_{k}$ we deduce that

$$ \eta_{\text{min}}:=\min_{j\in[s]}\inf_{x\notin[x_{j}^{\star}-\eta_{\varepsilon},x_{j}^{\star}+\eta_{\varepsilon}]}|\nu(x)|>0. $$

On the other, hand

$$ \eta_{\text{max}}:=\sup_{|x|<M}|x(\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x))|<\infty $$

is finite, since it is the restriction of a polynomial to a compact interval. Note that $\eta_{\text{min}},\eta_{\text{max}}$ depend only on $r,c,\omega_{0},\omega_{1},\dots\omega_{s}$ and $\delta_{1},\dots,\delta_{s}$ . Since $\sigma_{i}^{2}\to\infty$ we can choose $i\geq N_{\varepsilon}$ such that

$$ \sigma_{i}^{2}>\frac{r^{2}\eta_{\text{max}}}{c\eta_{\text{min}}} $$

Let $z$ be any real root of $Q_{i}$ . From Lemma E.4 and Lemma E.5 we know that $\min_{j\in[s]}|z-x_{j}^{\star}|>\eta_{\varepsilon}$ and $|z|<M$ . Suppose for the sake of contradiction that

$$ P_{i}(z)=z(\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(z))+c\,\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{r^{2}}\nu(z)=0. $$

This implies

$$ c\,\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{r^{2}}\eta_{\text{min}}\leq c\,\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{r^{2}}|\nu(z)|=\left|z(\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(z))\right|\leq\eta_{\text{max}}, $$

which is a contradiction. Thus for $\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}=\sigma_{i}^{2}$ , $P$ and $Q$ do not share a root. Lemma E.1 now implies the conclusion. ∎

### E.2 Proof of Lemma E.1

#### Proof.

Recall from Lemma 3.3 that the spectral shrinkage function corresponding to a $t$ -step SD is

$$ f_{t}(x)=\frac{1-\xi_{t}}{x+\lambda_{t}}+\frac{\xi_{t}(1-\xi_{t-1})x}{(x+\lambda_{t})(x+\lambda_{t-1})}+\dots+\frac{\xi_{t}\dots\xi_{1}\,x^{t}}{(x+\lambda_{t})(x+\lambda_{t-1})\dots(x+\lambda_{0})} $$

which, after raising to a common denominator, is the ratio of a polynomial $U(x)$ and a polynomial $V(x)$ with $\deg U\leq t$ and $\deg V=t+1$ . Recall from Lemma D.1 that $\deg P=s+1$ and $\deg Q=s$ . If $f_{t}=f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ , then

$$ \frac{Q(x)}{P(x)}=\frac{U(x)}{V(x)}, $$

hence $P(x)U(x)=Q(x)V(x)$ and since $(P,Q)=1$ then $P(x)\mid V(x)$ so

$$ t+1=\deg V(x)\geq\deg P(x)=s+1. $$

This proves that one cannot achieve $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ with less than $s$ rounds of self-distillation. ∎

### E.3 Proof of Lemma E.2

#### Proof.

Recall from equation (E.1) that

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)=g(x)-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}A_{j}h_{j}(x), $$

so taking the $xw(x)$ -inner product (B.2) with $h_{k}$ we have

$$ A_{k}=\langle g,h_{k}\rangle_{w}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}A_{j}\langle h_{j},h_{k}\rangle_{w}. $$

From equation (B.1) we know

$$ g(x)=\frac{r^{2}}{w(x)}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}h_{j}(x), $$

thus

$$ \displaystyle\langle g,h_{k}\rangle_{w} \displaystyle=\int{r^{2}xh_{k}(x)}\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\langle h_{j},h_{k}\rangle_{w} \displaystyle=\int\frac{r^{2}x\mu_{k}(x)}{w(x)}\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\langle h_{j},h_{k}\rangle_{w} \displaystyle=\underbrace{\int\frac{r^{2}x}{w(x)}\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{k}}(x)}_{\Delta_{k}}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\langle h_{j},h_{k}\rangle_{w}. $$

We deduce that

$$ A_{k}=\Delta_{k}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}(1-A_{j})\langle h_{j},h_{k}\rangle_{w}. $$

Recall $\bm{H}$ and $\mathfrak{D}$ from section B.3. Let $\mathfrak{D}_{-}$ be $\mathfrak{D}$ without the first entry. In matrix form, the system above is

$$ \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}1+\delta_{1}\alpha_{1}^{2}\langle h_{1},h_{1}\rangle_{w}&\cdots&\delta_{s}\alpha_{s}^{2}\langle h_{s},h_{1}\rangle_{w}\\
\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
\delta_{1}\alpha_{1}^{2}\langle h_{1},h_{s}\rangle_{w}&\cdots&1+\delta_{s}\alpha_{s}^{2}\langle h_{s},h_{s}\rangle_{w}\end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf{I}_{s}+\bm{H}\mathfrak{D}_{-}}\begin{pmatrix}1-A_{1}\\
\vdots\\
1-A_{s}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1-\Delta_{1}\\
\vdots\\
1-\Delta_{s}\end{pmatrix}. $$

This means

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}1-A_{1}\\
\vdots\\
1-A_{s}\end{pmatrix}=({\mathbf{I}_{s}+\bm{H}\mathfrak{D}_{-}})^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}1-\Delta_{1}\\
\vdots\\
1-\Delta_{s}\end{pmatrix}, $$

or equivalently

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{-}^{1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1-A_{1}\\
\vdots\\
1-A_{s}\end{pmatrix}=(\mathbf{I}_{s}+\mathfrak{D}_{-}^{1/2}\bm{H}\mathfrak{D}_{-}^{1/2})^{-1}\mathfrak{D}_{-}^{1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1-\Delta_{1}\\
\vdots\\
1-\Delta_{s}\end{pmatrix}. $$

As proved in Section B.3, $\mathfrak{D}_{-}^{1/2}\bm{H}\mathfrak{D}_{-}^{1/2}$ is positive-definite, so the operator norm of the inverse is

$$ \|({\mathbf{I}_{s}+\mathfrak{D}_{-}^{1/2}\bm{H}\mathfrak{D}_{-}^{1/2}})^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{2}}\leq 1. $$

We deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}(1-A_{j})^{2}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}(1-\Delta_{j})^{2}. $$

Next, we prove that $\Delta_{k}\in(0,1)$ for all $k\in[s]$ , thus equation (E.4) implies that all terms in the right hand side are $\leq 1$ , hence proving Lemma E.2. Recall from the previous section A.11 that $F_{\delta_{k}}$ is a probability measure that is absolutely continuous on $\mathcal{S}_{c}=((1-\sqrt{c})^{2},(1+\sqrt{c})^{2})$ and has two possible atoms

$$ F_{\delta_{k}}(\{0\})=\frac{c-1}{c+\delta_{k}}\cdot\mathbf{1}[c>1]\qquad F_{\delta_{k}}(x_{k}^{\star})=\frac{\delta_{k}^{2}-c}{\delta_{k}(c+\delta_{k})}\cdot\mathbf{1}[\delta_{k}>\sqrt{c}] $$

Since $w(x)=r^{2}x+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)>r^{2}x$ in the bulk and $\mu_{0}(x_{k}^{\star})=0$ , it is clear that $1>\Delta_{k}>0$ . ∎

### E.4 Proof of Lemma E.3

#### Proof.

We start by proving the following limit:

$$ \lim_{{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}\to\infty}\langle h_{i},h_{j}\rangle_{w}=\frac{\delta_{i}^{2}-c}{\alpha_{i}^{2}\delta_{i}(\delta_{i}+c)}\cdot\mathbf{1}[i=j]. $$

By definition of the $xw(x)$ -inner product and A.14, we have

$$ \langle h_{i},h_{j}\rangle_{w}=\int xw(x)h_{i}(x)h_{j}(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}=\int\frac{x\mu_{j}(x)}{w(x)}\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{i}}=\int\frac{x\mu_{j}(x)}{r^{2}x+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)}\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{i}}. $$

Recall that $\mu_{0}(x_{i}^{\star})=0$ and $\mu_{j}(x_{i}^{\star})=0$ if $i\neq j$ and $\omega_{i}^{-1}$ if $i=j$ . We deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\langle h_{i},h_{j}\rangle_{w} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{S}_{c}}\frac{x\mu_{j}(x)}{r^{2}x+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)}\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{i}}+\frac{\delta_{i}^{2}-c}{\delta_{i}(\delta_{i}+c)}\cdot\frac{x\mu_{j}(x_{i}^{\star})}{r^{2}x_{i}^{\star}}\cdot\mathbf{1}[i=j] \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{S}_{c}}\frac{x\mu_{j}(x)}{r^{2}x+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)}\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{i}}+\frac{\delta_{i}^{2}-c}{\alpha_{i}^{2}\delta_{i}(\delta_{i}+c)}\cdot\mathbf{1}[i=j]. $$

Since $\mu_{0}(x)\neq 0$ for $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}$ , conclusion follows by Dominated Convergence.

Similarly, we can conclude that

$$ \lim_{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\to\infty}\Delta_{i}=\frac{\delta_{i}^{2}-c}{\delta_{i}(\delta_{i}+c)}. $$

Taking limits as $\sigma^{2}\to\infty$ along $\{\sigma_{k}^{2}\}_{k=1}^{\infty}$ in (E.2) yields

$$ \displaystyle A_{k}^{\infty} \displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{k}^{2}-c}{\delta_{k}(\delta_{k}+c)}+\delta_{k}\alpha_{k}^{2}(1-A_{k}^{\infty})\cdot\frac{\delta_{k}^{2}-c}{\alpha_{k}^{2}\delta_{k}(\delta_{k}+c)} \displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{k}^{2}-c}{\delta_{k}(\delta_{k}+c)}+\frac{\delta_{k}^{2}-c}{\delta_{k}+c}(1-A_{k}^{\infty}), $$

which by straightforward algebraic manipulations is equivalent to

$$ A_{k}^{\infty}=1-\frac{c}{\delta_{k}^{2}}. $$

In particular, for $i$ large enough we have $1-A_{k}^{\sigma_{i}}>0$ for all $k\in[s]$ and since

$$ \delta_{k}|1-A_{k}^{\infty}|=\frac{c}{\delta_{k}}<\frac{1}{2}, $$

we can choose $i$ large enough so that the inequality above is also true for all $A_{k}^{\sigma_{i}}$ . ∎

### E.5 Proof of Lemma E.4

#### Proof.

Fix some $\varepsilon>0$ that we will choose later. Note that $Q_{\infty}(x)$ is a polynomial so there exists $\eta_{\varepsilon}>0$ such that

$$ \max_{j\in[s]}\sup_{x\in[x_{j}^{\star}-\eta_{\varepsilon},x_{j}^{\star}+\eta_{\varepsilon}]}|Q_{\infty}(x)-Q_{\infty}(x_{j}^{\star})|\leq\varepsilon. $$

Consider the interval $I_{\varepsilon}=[x_{1}^{\star}-\eta_{\varepsilon},x_{s}^{\star}+\eta_{\varepsilon}]$ . Note that $\nu_{-1},\dots,\nu_{-s}$ are continuous polynomial functions so there exists $M_{\varepsilon}>0$ such that

$$ \max_{j\in[s]}\sup_{x\in I_{\varepsilon}}|\nu_{-j}(x)|\leq M_{\varepsilon}. $$

By triangle inequality, note that

$$ |Q_{i}(x)-Q_{\infty}(x)|\leq\sum_{j=1}^{s}|\delta_{j}\omega_{j}(A_{j}^{\infty}-A_{j}^{\sigma_{i}})\nu_{-j}(x)|\leq\sum_{j=1}^{s}M_{\varepsilon}|\delta_{j}\omega_{j}||A_{j}^{\infty}-A_{j}^{\sigma_{i}}|. $$

Recall that $A_{j}^{\sigma_{i}}\to A_{j}^{\infty}$ as $i\to\infty$ for all $j$ . Since $\{\delta_{k},\omega_{k}\}_{k}$ are fixed, we deduce that there exists $N_{\varepsilon}$ such that

$$ \sup_{x\in I_{\varepsilon}}|Q_{i}(x)-Q_{\infty}(x)|\leq\varepsilon $$

for all $i\geq N_{\varepsilon}$ . Choose $i\geq N_{\varepsilon}$ and let $z$ be a real root of $Q_{i}$ . Assume that $z\in[x_{k}^{\star}-\eta_{\varepsilon},x_{k}^{\star}+\eta_{\varepsilon}]\subseteq I_{\varepsilon}$ for some $k\in[s]$ . We deduce that

$$ |Q_{\infty}(x_{k}^{\star})|\leq|Q_{\infty}(x_{k}^{\star})-Q_{\infty}(z)|+|Q_{\infty}(z)-Q_{i}(z)|\leq\varepsilon+\varepsilon=2\varepsilon. $$

However, by definition

$$ Q_{\infty}(x_{k}^{\star})=\omega_{k}\nu_{-k}(x_{k}^{\star})\left[1+\delta_{k}(1-A_{k}^{\infty})\right]. $$

Finally, using the main assumption we have $\delta_{k}|1-A_{k}^{\infty}|\leq 1/2$ , so

$$ 1+\delta_{k}(1-A_{k}^{\infty})\geq 1-|\delta_{k}(1-A_{k}^{\infty})|\geq 1/2. $$

This means that

$$ \left|\frac{\omega_{k}\nu_{-k}(x_{k}^{\star})}{2}\right|\leq|Q_{\infty}(x_{k}^{\star})|\leq 2\varepsilon. $$

Thus if we choose

$$ \varepsilon=\min_{k\in[s]}\left|\frac{\omega_{k}\nu_{-k}(x_{k}^{\star})}{8}\right|>0, $$

we obtain a contradiction, and the proof is complete. ∎

### E.6 Proof of Lemma E.5

#### Proof.

Fix any $i\geq N_{\varepsilon}$ . First, recall from equation (E.7) that $1+\delta_{k}(1-A_{k}^{\sigma_{i}})>1/2>0$ .

We deduce that $Q_{i}(x_{k}^{\star})=\omega_{k}\nu_{-k}(x_{k}^{\star})(1+\delta_{k}(1-A_{k}^{\sigma_{i}}))$ . Since the second term is positive, we deduce that $Q_{i}(x_{k}^{\star})$ has the same sign as $(-1)^{k-1}$ since

$$ \nu_{1}(x_{k}^{\star}),\dots,\nu_{k-1}(x_{k}^{\star})<0<\nu_{k+1}(x_{k}^{\star}),\dots,\nu_{s}(x_{k}^{\star}) $$

(see D.2 for a similar argument). In particular, there is a root $z_{k}$ of $Q_{i}$ such that $x_{k}^{\star}<z_{k}<x_{k+1}^{\star}$ . This gives us $s-1$ real roots. By Vieta’s formula the other root must also be real $z_{s}$ and we have

$$ Q_{i}(0)=r^{2}\omega_{0}(-1)^{s}\prod_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}}{c(\delta_{j}+1)}(-1)^{s}z_{1}\dots z_{s}=r^{2}\omega_{0}\prod_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}}{c(\delta_{j}+1)}z_{1}\dots z_{s}. $$

On the other hand, we can evaluate directly using $\nu_{j}(0)=(\delta_{j}+c)/c,$

$$ Q_{i}(0)=\omega_{0}\nu(0)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\frac{\nu(0)}{\nu_{j}(0)}(1+\delta_{j}(1-A_{j}^{\sigma_{i}}))=\prod_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}+c}{c}\left(\omega_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{c\,\omega_{j}}{\delta_{j}+c}(1+\delta_{j}(1-A_{j}^{\sigma_{i}}))\right). $$

In particular, it is immediate that $z_{s}>0$ . Moreover, using $z_{k}>x_{k}^{\star}$ for $k<s$ , we deduce that

$$ \prod_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}+c}{c}\left(\omega_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{c\,\omega_{j}}{\delta_{j}+c}(1+\delta_{j}(1-A_{j}^{\sigma_{i}}))\right)>r^{2}\omega_{0}\prod_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}}{c(\delta_{j}+1)}x_{1}^{\star}\dots x_{s-1}^{\star}z_{s}=r^{2}z_{s}\,\omega_{0}\prod_{j=1}^{s-1}\frac{\delta_{j}+c}{c} $$

using the definition of $x_{k}^{\star}$ . We conclude that

$$ 0<z_{s}<\frac{1}{{r^{2}\omega_{0}}}\cdot\frac{\delta_{s}+c}{c}\cdot\left(\omega_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{c\,\omega_{j}}{\delta_{j}+c}(1+\delta_{j}(1-A_{j}^{\sigma_{i}}))\right) $$

and since the $|1-A_{j}^{\sigma_{i}}|$ ’s are bounded by (E.4) for all $i\geq N_{\varepsilon}$ , the conclusion follows. ∎

## Appendix F $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ versus other Estimators - Proofs of Theorems 3.5(a), (b) and (c)

As discussed in Section 3, many of the common estimators used in practice correspond to or are well-approximated by simple shrinkage rules. In this section, we prove Theorem 3.5 parts (a), (b) and (c) i.e., the shrinkage rule $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ we computed in Appendix B achieves a strictly smaller loss than the min-norm interpolator, self-distillation shrinkage rules that use the same $\lambda$ for all rounds of distillation (in particular Ridge Regression) and finally, early stopped gradient descent.

### F.1 Notation

We consider the SVD decomposition $\bm{X}=\bm{U}\bar{\bm{S}}\bm{W}^{\top},$ where $\bm{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ has orthogonal columns, $\bm{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ is orthogonal, and $\bar{\bm{S}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ is rectangular diagonal with singular values $\bar{s}_{1}\geq\dots\geq\bar{s}_{\min\{n,p\}}>0$ on the main diagonal (and zeros elsewhere), where $\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\min\{n,p\}$ a.s. Recall that the sample covariance matrix is

$$ \widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}=\frac{1}{n}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}=\frac{1}{n}\bm{W}\bar{\bm{S}}^{\top}\bar{\bm{S}}\bm{W}^{\top}=\bm{W}\bm{\Lambda}\bm{W}^{\top}, $$

where $d_{j}=\bar{s}_{j}^{2}/n.$ Since

$$ \bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}=(\bm{U}\bar{\bm{S}}\bm{W}^{\top})^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{W}\bar{\bm{S}}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\bar{s}_{j}\bm{w}_{j}(\bm{u}_{j}^{\top}\bm{y}), $$

for any function $f\in\mathcal{F}$ we have

$$ f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}}{n}=\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{W}\bar{\bm{S}}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}}{n}=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{f(d_{j})\bar{s}_{j}}{n}\bm{w}_{j}(\bm{u}_{j}^{\top}\bm{y}). $$

### F.2 Proof of Theorem 3.5(a)

Consider the min-norm interpolator

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{mn}}={\arg\min}_{\bm{\beta}}\{\|{\bm{\beta}}\|_{2}:\bm{X}{\bm{\beta}}=\bm{y}\}. $$

In particular, if $n>p$ then $\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{mn}}=\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{OLS}}$ a.s. Using the notations introduced in Appendix F.1, it is well-known that

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{mn}}=\sum_{j=1}^{\min\{n,p\}}\frac{\bm{u}_{j}^{\top}\bm{y}}{\bar{s}_{j}}\bm{w}_{j}. $$

It is well-known [29] that the asymptotic risk of the min-norm interpolator is infinite for $c=1$ , so work with $c\neq 1$ . The key claim that proves that $\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{mn}}$ has a larger prediction risk than $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ is the following Lemma.

#### Lemma F.1.

There exists $f_{0}\in\mathcal{F}$ such that $f_{0}\not\equiv f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ in $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}\setminus\{0\}$ and

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{mn}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{=}}\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f_{0};c). $$

The proof of Theorem 3.5(a) now follows from Lemma B.3.

### F.3 Proof of Theorem 3.5(b)

The key step is to reduce the proof to the $0$ -step estimator, which is not optimal, as shown by the following lemma.

#### Lemma F.2.

Assume $s\geq 1$ . Then $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ has strictly smaller risk than any Ridge estimator with $-\lambda\notin\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ .

Using this Lemma, the proof of Theorem 3.5(b) becomes purely algebraic.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.5(b).

Suppose for contradiction that there exists an SD procedure that uses the same $\lambda$ at each step and achieves prediction risk no greater than that of $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ .

Recall from Lemma 3.3 that any SD procedure with $\lambda:=\lambda_{0}=\lambda_{1}=\dots=\lambda_{t}$ corresponds to a shrinkage function $f_{t}\in\mathcal{F}$ given by

$$ f_{t}(x)=\frac{1-\xi_{t}}{x+\lambda}+\frac{\xi_{t}(1-\xi_{t-1})x}{(x+\lambda)^{2}}+\dots+\frac{\xi_{t}\xi_{t-1}\dots\xi_{2}(1-\xi_{1})\,x^{t-1}}{(x+\lambda)^{t}}+\frac{\xi_{t}\dots\xi_{1}\,x^{t}}{(x+\lambda)^{t+1}}, $$

which after raising to a common denominator is

$$ f_{t}(x)=\frac{U(x)}{(x+\lambda)^{t+1}}, $$

for some monic polynomial with real coefficients $U(x)$ with $\deg U=t$ as

$$ (1-\xi_{t})+\xi_{t}(1-\xi_{t-1})+\dots+\xi_{t}\xi_{t-1}\dots\xi_{2}(1-\xi_{1})+\xi_{t}\xi_{t-1}\dots\xi_{2}\xi_{1}=1. $$

Recall from Lemma D.1 that

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)=\frac{Q(x)}{P(x)}, $$

where $P$ has $s+1$ distinct real roots. Since $f_{t}\in\mathcal{F}$ and $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ achieves the smallest risk across all function in $\mathcal{F}$ then they must have equal asymptotic risk. Thus, by Lemma B.3

$$ \frac{Q(x)}{P(x)}=\frac{U(x)}{(x+\lambda)^{t+1}}, $$

for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}$ . Equivalently, we have $Q(x)(x+\lambda)^{t+1}=U(x)P(x)$ . Since this is a polynomial equation that holds for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}$ which is infinite, then it must hold for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$ . Since $P$ has $s+1$ distinct roots, then $(x+\lambda)^{2}\nmid P(x)$ so $(x+\lambda)^{t}\mid U(x)$ . Since $U$ is monic, we deduce that we must have $U(x)=(x+\lambda)^{t}$ hence

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)=\frac{Q(x)}{P(x)}=\frac{1}{x+\lambda}, $$

which is a contradiction to Lemma F.2.

∎

### F.4 Proof of Theorem 3.5(c)

Consider gradient descent applied to the squared error loss

$$ \mathcal{L}_{n}({\bm{\beta}})=\frac{1}{2n}\|\bm{y}-\bm{X}{\bm{\beta}}\|_{2}^{2}. $$

The gradient is

$$ \nabla\mathcal{L}_{n}({\bm{\beta}})=-\frac{1}{n}\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}{\bm{\beta}})=\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}{\bm{\beta}}-\frac{1}{n}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}. $$

Thus, gradient descent with step size $\eta>0$ updates as

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{t+1}=\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{t}-\eta\nabla\mathcal{L}_{n}(\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{t})=\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{t}+\eta\frac{1}{n}\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{t})=(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\eta\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{t}+\eta\frac{1}{n}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}. $$

Suppose we initialize at $\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{0}=0$ and run gradient descent for $T$ steps. Unravelling the recursion yields:

$$ \widehat{\beta}_{T}=(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\eta\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})^{T}\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\eta\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\eta\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})^{k}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}}{n}. $$

Since $\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{0}=0$ , this simplifies to

$$ \widehat{\beta}_{T}=\eta\left(\mathbf{I}_{p}+(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\eta\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})+\cdots+(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\eta\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})^{T-1}\right)\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}}{n}=\bm{W}\,f_{T}(\bm{\Lambda})\,\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}}{n}, $$

where the shrinkage function $f_{T}$ is:

$$ f_{T}(x)=\eta\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}(1-\eta x)^{k}=\eta\left(1+(1-\eta x)+\cdots+(1-\eta x)^{T-1}\right), $$

which is a polynomial in $x$ of degree $T-1$ . In particular, $f_{T}$ is not equal to rational functions $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ or $f_{\ast}^{\text{ast}}$ . By Lemma B.3, we deduce that early-stopped gradient descent is suboptimal.

### F.5 Proof of Lemma F.1

#### Proof.

We distinguish between the two cases $c>1$ and $c<1$ . Assume for now that $c>1$ and without loss of generality that $p>n$ . Let $0<\eta<\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\sqrt{c}-1)^{2}$ be fixed and define $f_{0}:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{R}$ by

$$ f_{0}(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in[0,\eta/2),\\[4.0pt]
\dfrac{1}{x},&x\in\big(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1-\sqrt{c})^{2}-\eta/2,\infty\big),\end{cases} $$

and interpolate smoothly on $(\eta/2,\,\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\sqrt{c}-1)^{2}-\eta/2)$ so that $f_{0}$ is smooth on $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ . Since $f_{*}^{\rm pred}$ does not have an atom at $0$ , we have $f_{0}\neq f_{*}^{\rm pred}$ on the support $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ .

Next, we claim that there exists an event $\Omega_{0}$ of probability one such that

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{mn}}(n,\omega)=\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f_{0}}(n,\omega) $$

for all $\omega\in\Omega_{0}$ and all $n\geq N(\omega)$ . Recall from [68] that

$$ d_{n+1}=\cdots=d_{p}=0,\qquad d_{n}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1-\sqrt{c})^{2}, $$

where $d_{1}\geq\cdots\geq d_{p}$ are the eigenvalues of $\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}$ . Let $\Omega_{0}$ be the event of probability one on which this convergence holds. Then for every $\omega\in\Omega_{0}$ , there exists $N(\omega)$ such that

$$ d_{n}(n,\omega)>\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\sqrt{c}-1)^{2}-\eta/2 $$

for all $n\geq N(\omega)$ . In particular, for all such $n$ , every nonzero eigenvalue of $\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}$ lies in the region where $f_{0}(x)=1/x$ , while the zero eigenvalues lie in the region where $f_{0}(x)=0$ . Therefore, using (F.1), for all $n\geq N(\omega)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle f_{0}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}}{n} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{f_{0}(d_{j})\,\bar{s}_{j}}{n}\,\bm{w}_{j}(\bm{u}_{j}^{\top}\bm{y}) \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\bar{s}_{j}}{nd_{j}}\,\bm{w}_{j}(\bm{u}_{j}^{\top}\bm{y})+\sum_{j=n+1}^{p}0\cdot\frac{\bar{s}_{j}}{n}\,\bm{w}_{j}(\bm{u}_{j}^{\top}\bm{y}) \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\bar{s}_{j}}\,\bm{w}_{j}(\bm{u}_{j}^{\top}\bm{y}). $$

Since $d_{j}=\bar{s}_{j}^{2}/n$ , the last expression is exactly the minimum-norm interpolator hence,

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f_{0}}(n,\omega)=\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{mn}}(n,\omega) $$

for all $\omega\in\Omega_{0}$ and all $n\geq N(\omega)$ . It follows that

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f_{0}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{=}}\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{mn}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2} $$

which proves the claim. The proof for $c<1$ follows mutatis mutandis using $d_{p}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1-\sqrt{c})^{2}$ . The details are omitted for brevity. ∎

### F.6 Proof of Lemma F.2

#### Proof.

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there was $\lambda$ such that the Ridge estimator with parameter $\lambda$ is at least as good as $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ . Since all Ridge estimators are in $\mathcal{F}$ , and $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ optimizes over $\mathcal{F}$ , the two shrinkage rules must have the same asymptotic risk. Assume without loss of generality that $x_{1}^{\star}=\min_{j}\{x_{j}^{\star}\}$ . Recall $P,Q$ from Lemma D.1 and note that we must have

$$ \frac{Q(x)}{P(x)}=\frac{1}{x+\lambda}, $$

or equivalently $Q(x)(x+\lambda)=P(x)$ for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}$ . This is a polynomial equation, so it must hold for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$ . In particular, $-\lambda$ must be a root of $P$ which from the proof of Lemma D.1 are either negative or greater than $x_{1}^{\star}$ . Thus $\lambda\neq 0$ . Using the formula from equation E.1 and Lemma B.3, we deduce that

$$ \frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\left(\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x)\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}(1-A_{j})\nu_{-j}(x)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}x\left(\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x)\right)+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\nu(x)}=\frac{1}{x+\lambda}. $$

From equation E.1 we also know

$$ A_{1}=\langle f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}},h_{1}\rangle_{w}=\int f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)h_{1}(x)xw(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}. $$

Using equation (B.1) and Lemma A.14, we can rewrite the equality above as

$$ \displaystyle A_{1} \displaystyle=\int f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)\,\frac{\mu_{1}(x)}{w(x)}\,x\,w(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle=\int xf_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)\,\mu_{1}(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle=\int xf_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{1}}(x) \displaystyle=\int\frac{x}{x+\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{1}}(x). $$

On the other hand, evaluating $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ at $x_{1}^{\star}$ yields

$$ \displaystyle f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{perd}}(x_{1}^{\star}) \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{1}\nu_{-1}(x_{1}^{\star})+\delta_{1}\alpha_{1}^{2}(1-A_{1})\nu_{-1}(x_{1}^{\star})}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x_{1}^{\star}\omega_{1}\nu_{-1}(x_{1}^{\star})} \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{1}(1-A_{1})}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,x_{1}^{\star}}, $$

since $r^{2}\omega_{1}=\alpha_{1}^{2}$ . Combining this equality with equation (F.2) we have

$$ \frac{1}{\lambda+x_{1}^{\star}}=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{1}\displaystyle\int\frac{\lambda}{x+\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{1}}(x)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,x_{1}^{\star}}, $$

which after multiplying both sides by $x_{1}^{\star}$ and rearranging yields

$$ \delta_{1}\int\frac{\lambda}{x+\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{1}}(x)=-\frac{\lambda\sigma_{0}^{2}\,}{\lambda+x_{1}^{\star}}. $$

Since $\lambda\neq 0$ we deduce that

$$ \delta_{1}\int\frac{1}{x+\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{1}}(x)=-\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,}{\lambda+x_{1}^{\star}}. $$

We consider two cases separately. If $\lambda>0$ then the left member is positive since all terms in the integral are positive, whereas the right member is negative, thus a contradiction.

If $\lambda<0$ , then $-\lambda>0$ is a positive root of $P$ , thus it must be larger than $x_{1}^{\star}>\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}$ or equivalently $x_{1}^{\star}+\lambda<0$ . Since $F_{\delta_{1}}$ has bulk $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ and two possible atoms at 0 and $x_{j}^{\star}$ (see Lemma A.11), then all terms in the integral above are negative, whereas the right member is positive, thus a contradiction. The proof is now complete. ∎

## Appendix G $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ versus PCR - Proofs of Theorems 3.5(d) and (e)

### G.1 Notation and General form of PCR

Throughout, we assume that

$$ m_{n}\leq{\sf rank}(\bm{X})=\min\{n,p\}, $$

since any additional components are redundant. Following [84] equation (25), define

$$ Q_{c}(x)=1-F_{\mathrm{MP}}(x), $$

and for $\tau^{\prime}\in\bigl[0,\min\{1,1/c\}\bigr]$ , let $Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau^{\prime})\in\mathcal{S}_{c}$ denote the unique value such that

$$ \int_{Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau^{\prime})}^{(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}}f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)\,dx=\tau^{\prime}. $$

It is well-known that if $m/p\to\tau\in(0,\min\{1,1/c\})$ then we can invert the quantiles at the continuity points (see [84]) to deduce that

$$ \displaystyle d_{m}\xrightarrow{a.s.}Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau). $$

We start by introducing standard notations for the PCR estimator. Let $\bm{U}_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ and $\bm{W}_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times m}$ denote the first $m$ columns of $\bm{U}$ and $\bm{W}$ , respectively, and let $\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}=\mathrm{diag}(s_{1},\dots,s_{m})$ . The $m$ -component PCR estimator is

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}=\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}\bm{y}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\bm{w}_{j}\frac{\bm{u}_{j}^{\top}\bm{y}}{\bar{s}_{j}}, $$

where $\bm{u}_{j}$ and $\bm{v}_{j}$ are the $j$ -th columns of $\bm{U}$ and $\bm{W}$ . Another way to obtain the PCR estimator is to define $\mathcal{P}_{m}:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R}^{p}$ be the projection onto the $m$ leading eigenspaces of $\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}$ ,

$$ \mathcal{P}_{m}=\bm{W}_{m}\bm{W}_{m}^{\top}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bm{w}_{i}\bm{w}_{i}^{\top}, $$

and likewise, let $\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}=\mathbf{I}_{p}-\mathcal{P}_{m}$ be the projection on the orthogonal space. First, using standard concentration results, we prove the following Lemma which will be used for both Theorem 3.5(d) and (e).

#### Lemma G.1.

If $m/p\to\tau\in[0,\min\{1,1/c\})$ , then as $n\to\infty$

$$ \|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}-\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}\mid\bm{X}\right]\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}0. $$

### G.2 Proof of Theorem 3.5(d)

In this section, we prove that $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ achieves smaller asymptotic than any PCR procedure that uses any fixed number of retained components $m_{n}=m$ . The proof is based on one Lemma that shows that if we wanted to perform better than $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ using PCR, we would need more components than the number of spikes that are above the BBP phase transition. Recall that $s^{+}\leq s$ is the number of $\delta_{j}$ ’s that are above the BBP phase transition.

#### Lemma G.2.

For all $m\leq s^{+}$ , there exists $f_{\text{pcr}}\in\mathcal{F}$ such that $f_{\text{pcr}}\not\equiv f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ on $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ and

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}=\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f_{\mathrm{pcr}};c). $$

Using this characterization of the prediction risk, we are ready to prove Theorem 3.5(d).

#### Proof of Theorem 3.5(d).

The key observation is that adding more than $s^{+}$ components is redundant in the limit. First, from Lemma G.1, we know that

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{a.s.}}}{{=}}\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}\mid\bm{X}\right]. $$

We can now compute the limit on the right-hand side of (G.3) using Theorem 3 in [84]. Indeed, for any $m\geq s^{+}$ , the contribution of the outliers vanishes in equation (59) of [84], so the limit no longer depends on $m$ . In particular,

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},s^{+}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}\mid\bm{X}\right]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{a.s.}}}{{=}}\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}\mid\bm{X}\right], $$

and combining this with Lemma G.1 applied to $s^{+}$ components and (G.3), we deduce that

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{a.s.}}}{{=}}\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},s^{+}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}. $$

Combining this with Lemma G.2 and Lemma B.3, we conclude that the asymptotic risk of PCR with finitely many components is strictly larger than that of $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ , thus completing the proof of Theorem 3.5(d). ∎

### G.3 Proof of Theorem 3.5(e)

In this section, we prove that $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ is strictly better than PCR with $m$ components for any sequence $m=m_{n}$ satisfying $m_{n}/p\to\tau\in\bigl[0,\min(1,1/c)\bigr)$ as $n\to\infty$ . The first observation is that, in the proportional regime, it is enough to restrict attention to the case $\tau\in\bigl(0,\min\{1,1/c\}\bigr).$ Indeed, if $\tau=0$ , then equation (59) in [84] implies that

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}\mid\bm{X}\right]=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},s^{+}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}\mid\bm{X}\right], $$

since in that case the contribution of the bulk vanishes in their formula. By Lemma G.3, we deduce that

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},s^{+}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2} $$

and by Lemma G.2 applied for $s^{+}$ components, the right term is strictly larger than the prediction risk of $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ . Thus, throughout this section, we will assume the following.

#### Assumption G.3.

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{m_{n}}{p}=\tau\in\bigl(0,\min\{1,1/c\}\bigr). $$

Since $\tau$ is assumed to be an interior value, it follows that $Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)\in\mathrm{int}(\mathcal{S}_{c}).$ We continue with the following lemma.

#### Lemma G.4.

Assume that G.3 holds. Then as $n\to\infty$ ,

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}\int_{0}^{Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)}\mathrm{d}F_{\tau}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\tau_{j}^{2}\int_{0}^{Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)}\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}(x)+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\int_{Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)}^{(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}}\frac{f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)}{x}\,dx. $$

Next, recall from Lemma B.1 that for a general function $f\in\mathcal{F}$ the asymptotic risk of $\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{a.s.}}}{{=}}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\int(1-xf(x))^{2}\ \mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)\ +\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\int(1-xf(x))\ \mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}(x)\right)^{2}+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\int xf^{2}(x)\ \mathrm{d}F_{\rm MP}(x)\,. $$

Using Lemma G.4, we deduce that the limit of $m$ -PCR is the same as that of

$$ f_{\text{PCR}}(x)=\begin{cases}0,\qquad\text{if }x<Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau),\\
1/x,\qquad\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Note that $f_{\mathrm{PCR}}$ is not continuous on $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ , and therefore $f_{\mathrm{PCR}}\notin\mathcal{F}$ . Thus, compared to the proofs of Lemma G.2 and Lemma F.1, extra work is required to conclude. The next technical Lemma proves that PCR is suboptimal to our $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ procedure.

#### Lemma G.5.

Assume G.3 holds. Then, there exists a uniformly bounded sequence of functions $\{f_{n}\}_{n}$ , with $f_{n}\in\mathcal{F}$ , and a constant $\eta>0$ such that:

- 1. $\lim_{n\to\infty}f_{n}(x)=f_{\mathrm{PCR}}(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ ,

- 2. $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f_{n};c)\geq\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}};c)+\eta$ .

Indeed, since the functions $f_{n}$ are uniformly bounded and the supports of $F_{\alpha}$ , $F_{\delta_{j}}$ , and $F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ are all bounded subsets of the nonnegative real line, we may apply the dominated convergence theorem using Lemma B.1 to deduce that

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f_{n})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}}. $$

Taking the limit as $n\to\infty$ in property 2 in the above Lemma completes the proof of Theorem 3.5(e).

### G.4 Proof of Lemma G.1

#### Proof.

For simplicity of notation, define

$$ T_{n}:=\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}. $$

Using $\bm{y}=\bm{X}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+{\bm{\varepsilon}}$ , we have

$$ \widehat{{\bm{\beta}}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}=\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}\bm{y}=\mathcal{P}_{m}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}, $$

so

$$ \widehat{{\bm{\beta}}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}=-\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}. $$

Therefore,

$$ T_{n}=\left\|\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\right\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}+\left\|\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}\right\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}-2\,\left(\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\right)^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}. $$

Since ${\bm{\varepsilon}}\perp\mkern-9.5mu\perp\bm{X}$ , $\mathbb{E}[{\bm{\varepsilon}}\mid\bm{X}]=0$ , and ${\sf cov}({\bm{\varepsilon}}\mid\bm{X})=\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{n},$ we obtain

$$ \displaystyle T_{n}-\mathbb{E}[T_{n}\mid\bm{X}] \displaystyle=-2\,\bigl(\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\bigr)^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\,\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}} \displaystyle+{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{\top}\bm{U}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{W}_{m}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\,\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}-\mathbb{E}\!\left[{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{\top}\bm{U}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{W}_{m}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\,\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}\,\middle|\,\bm{X}\right] \displaystyle=-2\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}\bm{\Sigma}\,\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}} \displaystyle+{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{\top}\bm{U}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{W}_{m}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\,\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}-\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}\,{\sf tr}\left(\bm{\Sigma}\,\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-2}\bm{W}_{m}^{\top}\right). $$

Finally, as in Section B.2, we use standard concentration results to show that both terms are negligible. Define

$$ \bm{a}_{n}=2n\,\bm{U}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{W}_{m}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, $$

so that the cross term equals $-\bm{a}_{n}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}/n$ . As in Section B.2, $\|\bm{W}_{m}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=1$ , and $\|\bm{\Sigma}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\max_{j\in[r]}\delta_{j}$ are all deterministically of order 1. Since $d_{i}=\bar{s}_{i}^{2}/n$ , we have

$$ \|\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=s_{m}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n\,d_{m}}}, $$

hence,

$$ \frac{\|\bm{a}_{n}\|_{2}^{2}}{n}\leq\frac{4\|\bm{\Sigma}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\,\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}{d_{m}}. $$

If $\tau=0$ , then there exists a small constant $\eta>0$ such that $d_{m}\geq d_{\lfloor p\eta\rfloor}$ for all large enough $n$ . Since the lower bound $d_{\lfloor p\eta\rfloor}$ converges to a point in $\text{int}\left(\mathcal{S}_{c}\right)$ , $d_{m}$ is almost surely bounded away from zero for all large $n$ . Similarly if $\tau>0$ , then $d_{m}\to Q^{-1}_{c}(\tau)\in\text{int}(\mathcal{S}_{c})$ almost surely, so $d_{m}$ is almost surely bounded away from zero for all large $n$ . In both cases, we can conclude that almost surely,

$$ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\|\bm{a}_{n}\|_{2}^{2}}{n}<\infty, $$

so we can apply Lemma A.16 to deduce that

$$ -2\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}\bm{\Sigma}\,\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}0. $$

Similarly, define

$$ \bm{A}_{n}=n\,\bm{U}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{W}_{m}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, $$

so that the quadratic term equals ${\bm{\varepsilon}}^{\top}\bm{A}_{n}{\bm{\varepsilon}}/n-\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}{\sf tr}(\bm{A}_{n})/n$ , since

$$ \frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{n}\,{\sf tr}(\bm{A}_{n})=\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\,{\sf tr}\left(\bm{\Sigma}\,\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-2}\bm{W}_{m}^{\top}\right), $$

where we used the cyclic property of the trace. Its operator norm satisfies

$$ \|\bm{A}_{n}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq n\,\|\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\,\|\bm{\Sigma}\|_{\mathrm{op}}, $$

which yields $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\|\bm{A}_{n}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$ by the same argument as above. Lemma A.17 gives

$$ {\bm{\varepsilon}}^{\top}\bm{U}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{W}_{m}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\,\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-1}\bm{U}_{m}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}-\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}\,{\sf tr}\left(\bm{\Sigma}\,\bm{W}_{m}\bar{\bm{S}}_{m}^{-2}\bm{W}_{m}^{\top}\right)=\frac{{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{\top}\bm{A}_{n}{\bm{\varepsilon}}}{n}-\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}{\sf tr}(\bm{A}_{n})}{n}\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}0, $$

thus completing the proof. ∎

### G.5 Proof of Lemma G.2

#### Proof.

We start with the case $m=s^{+}=1$ . Let $x_{1}^{\star}$ be the outlier that corresponds to $\delta_{1}>\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}$ as in Lemma A.6(b). Choose

$$ 0<\eta<x_{1}^{\star}-\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}. $$

As in the proof of Lemma F.1, we define $f_{\mathrm{pcr}}$ by

$$ f_{\mathrm{pcr}}(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{x},&x\in(x_{1}^{\star}-\eta/2,\;x_{1}^{\star}+\eta/2),\\[4.0pt]
0,&x\in[0,x_{1}^{\star}-\eta)\cup(x_{1}^{\star}+\eta,\infty)\end{cases}, $$

and interpolate smoothly on $(x_{1}^{\star}-\eta,\;x_{1}^{\star}-\eta/2)$ and $(x_{1}^{\star}+\eta/2,\;x_{1}^{\star}+\eta)$ so that $f_{\mathrm{pcr}}$ is smooth on $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ . Note that $f_{\mathrm{pcr}}\equiv 0$ on the bulk, whereas $f_{\ast}$ is not identically zero there. We now claim that there exists an event $\Omega$ of probability one such that

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f_{\mathrm{pcr}}}(n,\omega)=\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},1}(n,\omega) $$

for all $\omega\in\Omega$ and all $n\geq N(\omega)$ . Indeed, by [68],

$$ d_{1}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}x_{1}^{\star},\qquad d_{2}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2},\qquad d_{p}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\begin{cases}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1-\sqrt{c})^{2},&\text{if }c<1,\\[4.0pt]
0,&\text{if }c\geq 1.\end{cases} $$

Hence there exists an event $\Omega$ of probability one on which all of the above convergences hold simultaneously. For each $\omega\in\Omega$ , and all $n$ large enough, we have

$$ d_{1}(n,\omega)\in(x_{1}^{\star}-\eta/2,\;x_{1}^{\star}+\eta/2), $$

while

$$ d_{2}(n,\omega),\dots,d_{p}(n,\omega)\in[0,x_{1}^{\star}-\eta)\cup(x_{1}^{\star}+\eta,\infty). $$

By construction of $f_{\mathrm{pcr}}$ , it follows that for all such $n$ ,

$$ f_{\mathrm{pcr}}(d_{1})=\frac{1}{d_{1}},\qquad f_{\mathrm{pcr}}(d_{j})=0,\quad j\geq 2. $$

Using (F.1), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle f_{\mathrm{pcr}}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}}{n} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{f_{\mathrm{pcr}}(d_{j})\,\bar{s}_{j}}{n}\,\bm{w}_{j}(\bm{u}_{j}^{\top}\bm{y}) \displaystyle=\frac{\bar{s}_{1}}{nd_{1}}\,\bm{w}_{1}(u_{1}^{\top}\bm{y}). $$

Since $d_{1}=\bar{s}_{1}^{2}/n$ , this simplifies to

$$ f_{\mathrm{pcr}}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}}{n}=\frac{1}{\bar{s}_{1}}\,\bm{w}_{1}(u_{1}^{\top}\bm{y}), $$

which is exactly the one-component PCR estimator (G.2). Therefore,

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f_{\mathrm{pcr}}}(n,\omega)=\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},1}(n,\omega) $$

for all $\omega\in\Omega$ and all $n\geq N(\omega)$ . Consequently,

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},1}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f_{\mathrm{pcr}}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}, $$

and the conclusion follows.

The general case follows by the same argument. Since the outliers $x_{j}^{\star}$ are pairwise distinct by Lemma A.12, one can choose sufficiently small disjoint neighborhoods around each of them on which the shrinkage function equals $1/x$ , and then smoothly interpolate between these neighborhoods on the remainder of the domain. The extension is immediate and we omit the details. ∎

### G.6 Proof of Lemma G.4

#### Proof.

Using equation (47) in [84], we have the following bias-variance decomposition:

$$ \mathbb{E}\Big[\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}}\mid\bm{X}\Big]=\|{\bm{\Sigma}}^{1/2}\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}+\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{n}{\sf tr}\left((\mathcal{P}_{m}\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}\mathcal{P}_{m})^{\dagger}{\bm{\Sigma}}\right). $$

We use the following decomposition

$$ {\bm{\Sigma}}^{1/2}=\sigma_{0}\,\mathbf{I}_{p}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\left(\sqrt{\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,}-\sigma_{0}\,\right)\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}, $$

which is straightforward from the definition of ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ . We deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\Big\|{\bm{\Sigma}}^{1/2}\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\Big\|^{2} \displaystyle=\Big\|\sigma_{0}\,\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\bigl(\sqrt{\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}}-\sigma_{0}\bigr)\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\Big\|^{2} \displaystyle=\|\sigma_{0}\,\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\left(\sqrt{\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,}-\sigma_{0}\right)^{2}\bigl(\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\bigr)^{2}+\,2\sum_{j=1}^{s}\sigma_{0}\left(\sqrt{\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}}-\sigma_{0}\right)\bigl(\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\bigr)^{2} \displaystyle=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\|\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\bigl(\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\bigr)^{2}. $$

Using the measure $\widehat{B}_{n}$ from Lemma A.7, we obtain

$$ \frac{\|\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}}=\int_{[0,d_{m+1}]}d\widehat{B}_{n}(x). $$

Recall that $d_{m}\to Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)\in\mathrm{int}(\mathcal{S}_{c})$ almost surely. Moreover, $\widehat{B}_{n}\xrightarrow{d}F_{\alpha}$ almost surely by Lemma A.7. Therefore, since $Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)$ is not an atom of $F_{\alpha}$ , a standard limiting argument gives

$$ \int_{[0,d_{m})}d\widehat{B}_{n}(x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{a.s.}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\int_{0}^{Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)}\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x). $$

By the same argument, using the signed measures $\widehat{C}_{n}^{j}$ and their vague limits $F_{\delta_{j}}$ from A.8, we obtain

$$ \frac{\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}}{\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}}=\int_{[0,d_{m})}d\widehat{C}_{n}^{j}(x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{a.s.}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\int_{0}^{Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)}\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}(x). $$

Therefore,

$$ (\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0})^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{a.s.}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\int_{0}^{Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)}\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}(x)\right)^{2}. $$

Finally, by Theorem 3 in [84],

$$ \frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{n}{\sf tr}\left((\mathcal{P}_{m}\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}\mathcal{P}_{m})^{\dagger}{\bm{\Sigma}}\right)\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\int_{Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)}^{b}\frac{1}{x^{2}|\underline{m}(x)|^{2}}f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x, $$

where $\underline{m}$ is the companion Stieltjes transform of the Marchenko–Pastur law (see equation (A.2)). By Lemma A.1, we have

$$ c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\int_{Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)}^{b}\frac{1}{x^{2}|\underline{m}(x)|^{2}}f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\int_{Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)}^{b}\frac{f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)}{x}\,dx. $$

Combining the three limits with Lemma G.1 gives the result. ∎

### G.7 Proof of Lemma G.5

#### Proof.

Fix $\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1-\sqrt{c})^{2}<\eta<Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)$ . Choose $\mathfrak{e}_{n}\downarrow 0$ such that $Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)-\mathfrak{e}_{n}>\eta$ for all $n$ . Let $\psi_{n}:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to[0,1]$ be a smooth function satisfying

$$ \psi_{n}(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\leq Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)-\mathfrak{e}_{n},\\[4.0pt]
1,&x\geq Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)+\mathfrak{e}_{n},\end{cases} $$

and define

$$ f_{n}(x)=\frac{\psi_{n}(x)}{x}. $$

It is straightforward to check that $f_{n}\to f_{\mathrm{PCR}}(x)$ pointwise on $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ . Moreover, $\{f_{n}\}_{n}$ are smooth and uniformly bounded by $1/\eta$ , so Lemma G.5(1) is proved.

Next, we prove the second property. Recall from equation (B.15) that for any $f\in\mathcal{F}$ the limiting risk $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)$ is, up to an additive constant, equal to

$$ \left\langle\mathcal{A}(f-f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}),f-f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}\right\rangle_{w}-\langle Af_{\ast},f_{\ast}\rangle_{w}. $$

Using equation B.11, we can immediately deduce that

$$ \mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f_{n};c)-\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}};c)=\left\langle\mathcal{A}(f_{n}-f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}),f_{n}-f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}\right\rangle_{w}\geq\|f_{n}-f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}\|_{w}^{2}. $$

Recall from B.1 that $w(x)>0$ for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ and note that $f_{n}(x)=0$ for all $x\leq\eta$ . We deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\|f_{n}-f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}\|_{w}^{2} \displaystyle=\int x\,w(x)\bigl(f_{n}(x)-f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)\bigr)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle\geq\int_{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1-\sqrt{c})^{2}}^{\eta}x\,w(x)\bigl(f_{n}(x)-f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)\bigr)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle=\int_{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1-\sqrt{c})^{2}}^{\eta}x\,w(x)f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x). $$

Thus, we can define $\rho$ as the lower bound above, and note that $\rho>0$ because $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ cannot be constant 0 on $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ by Lemma D.1. ∎

## Appendix H Estimation Risk - Proof of Theorem 3.6

### H.1 Proof of Theorem 3.6(a) and (b)

In this section, we prove that the same ideas used for the Out-of-sample risk hold for estimation risk. We prove the first two steps of Theorem 3.6 following the steps of proof of Theorem 3.1 mutatis mutandis. First, we provide a general formula for $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{est}}(f;c)$ that holds for all $f\in\mathcal{F}$ .

#### Lemma H.1.

For any $f\in\mathcal{F}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{est}}(f;c) \displaystyle\overset{a.s.}{=}r^{2}\int(1-xf(x))^{2}\ \mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)+c{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}\int xf^{2}(x)\ \mathrm{d}F_{\rm MP}(x). $$

Note that the formula is very similar to that in Lemma B.1 for the prediction risk, the only difference being the absence of the squared integrals terms. This significantly simplifies the process of finding $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{est}}$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 3.6(a) and (b).

Recall $w(x),g(x)$ and $\mu_{j}(x)$ from (B.1). Expanding everything in the formula from Lemma H.1 we have:

$$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{est}}(f;c)&=r^{2}-2r^{2}\int x\,f(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)+r^{2}\int x^{2}f(x)^{2}\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}+c\,{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}\int xf^{2}(x)\ \mathrm{d}F_{\rm MP}(x)\\
&=r^{2}+\int\Bigl(r^{2}x^{2}+c\,\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}\,x\,\mu_{0}(x)\Bigr)\,f(x)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)-2r^{2}\int x\,f(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)\\
&=r^{2}+\int\left[\left(r^{2}x^{2}+c\,\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}\,x\,\mu_{0}(x)\right)\,f(x)^{2}-2r^{2}x\,f(x)\right]\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)\end{aligned}, $$

where we used the Radon-Nikodym derivative $\mu_{0}$ of $F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ w.r.t. $F_{\alpha}$ from Lemma A.14. Note that for each $x$ the integrand is a quadratic in $f(x)$ which is uniquely minimized for $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}\setminus\{0\}$ at

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{est}}(x)=\frac{r^{2}}{r^{2}x+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)}=\frac{r^{2}\left(\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x)\right)}{r^{2}x\left(\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x)\right)+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\nu(x)}. $$

Uniqueness follows, since any function that achieves equality must agree with the minimum of the quadratic on a set of $F_{\alpha}$ -measure $1$ . Since the functions must be continuous, this proves part (a).

Next, note that the denominator of $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{est}}(x)$ is the same as the denominator of $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ up to a factor of $\sigma_{0}^{2}$ (see Theorem 3.1). Thus, using Lemma D.1 we know that the denominator has $s+1$ real roots, and a similar application of Lemma D.2 yields the first part of Theorem 3.6(b). We omit the details.

Finally, we prove that $s$ steps are always necessary to achieve $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{est}}$ . Note that any common root of the denominator and numerator in the display above must also be a root of $\nu(x)$ . Recall from Lemma A.11 that the only roots of

$$ \nu(x)=\nu_{1}(x)\cdot\nu_{2}(x)\cdots\nu_{s}(x) $$

are the outliers $x_{1}^{\star},\dots,x_{s}^{\star}$ . However, by Lemma D.1, we know that the denominator has exactly $s+1$ real roots that lie outside $\overline{\mathcal{S}_{c}}$ . In particular, $x_{1}^{\star},\dots,x_{s}^{\star}$ can not be common roots, so by the same method as in Lemma E.1 conclusion follows. ∎

### H.2 Proof of Theorem 3.6(c)

#### Proof.

The proofs that $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{est}}$ achieves smaller risk than the min-norm interpolator, early stopped gradient descent and PCR with a fixed number of components follow mutatis mutandis from their corresponding Theorems for prediction risk. We omit the details for brevity.

Next, as proved in the previous section, the denominator $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{est}}$ has $s+1$ distinct, real roots and the rational function is irreducible. In particular, Ridge regression is suboptimal and so is any procedure that uses the same $\lambda$ across distillation steps.

Finally, the only case left is PCR with diverging number of retained components. As before, we work under Assumption G.3. Using the same concentration inequalities as in Lemma G.1, we infer that

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}_{2}\,\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{a.s.}}}{{=}}\,\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}_{2}\mid\bm{X}\Big], $$

where we omit the details for the sake of brevity. Thus, it is enough to work with the conditional asymptotic risk. From equation (27) in [84],

$$ \mathbb{E}\Big[\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{PCR},m}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}_{2}\mid\bm{X}\Big]=\|\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}+\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{n}{\sf tr}\left((\mathcal{P}_{m}\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}\mathcal{P}_{m})^{\dagger}\right). $$

As proved in Lemma G.4, the limit of the bias term is

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\|\mathcal{P}_{m}^{\perp}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}\,\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{a.s.}}}{{=}}\,r^{2}\int_{0}^{Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)}\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x), $$

and using Theorem 1 in [84]

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{n}{\sf tr}\left((\mathcal{P}_{m}\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}\mathcal{P}_{m})^{\dagger}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{a.s.}}}{{=}}\,c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\int_{Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)}^{(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}}\frac{f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x. $$

As in the prediction error case, the limit of $m$ -PCR is the same as that of

$$ f_{\text{PCR}}(x)=\begin{cases}0,\qquad\text{if }x<Q_{c}^{-1}(\tau)\\
1/x,\qquad\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

We can now finish using the same approximation as in Lemma G.5. This completes the proof of Theorem 3.6(c). ∎

### H.3 Proof of Lemma H.1

#### Proof.

Recall from (B.4) that:

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f}=\bm{W}(\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda}))\bm{W}^{\top}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}}{n}. $$

Therefore, following the same ideas as in Section B.2,

$$ \displaystyle\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle={\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)^{2}\bm{W}^{\top}{\bm{\beta}}_{0} \displaystyle\quad-2\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}}{n} \displaystyle\quad+\frac{\bm{\varepsilon}^{\top}\bm{X}}{n}\bm{W}f^{2}(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}}{n}, $$

where we used $\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W}=\mathbf{I}_{p}$ . Alternatively,

$$ \|\widehat{{\bm{\beta}}}_{f}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}=\mathcal{B}_{f}^{\mathrm{est}}(\bm{X},\bm{y})+\mathcal{V}_{f}^{\mathrm{est}}(\bm{X},\bm{y})+\mathcal{E}_{f,n}^{\mathrm{est}}(\bm{X},\bm{y}), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{f}^{\mathrm{est}}(\bm{X},\bm{y}) \displaystyle:={\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)^{2}\bm{W}^{\top}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}, \displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{f}^{\mathrm{est}}(\bm{X},\bm{y}) \displaystyle:=\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{n^{2}}{\sf tr}\left(\bm{X}f^{2}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\bm{X}^{\top}\right)=\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{n}{\sf tr}\left(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}f^{2}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\right), \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{f}^{\mathrm{est}}(\bm{X},\bm{y}) \displaystyle:=-2\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}}{n}+\left[\frac{{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{\top}\bm{X}f^{2}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\bm{X}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}}{n^{2}}-\mathcal{V}_{f}^{\mathrm{est}}(\bm{X},\bm{y})\right]. $$

Note that for all sufficiently large $n$ we can rewrite the bias term using the empirical measures introduced in Appendix A.5 as

$$ \mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{est}}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y}):=\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}\int\left(1-xf(x)\right)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\widehat{B}_{n}(x). $$

Using Lemma A.7 and Lemma A.15, we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{est}}_{f}\xrightarrow{a.s.}r^{2}\int(1-xf(x))^{2}\ \mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x). $$

Consider now the variance term and note that for all sufficiently large $n$ we can rewrite it as

$$ \mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{est}}_{f}=\frac{{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}\,p}{n}\int xf^{2}(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}}(x). $$

Using Lemma A.6 and Lemma A.9, we know that $F_{\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}}\xrightarrow{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ and $\widehat{D}_{n}^{j}\xrightarrow{d}F_{\delta_{j}}$ . Using Lemma A.15 and Lemma A.15 again, we know that

$$ \mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{est}}_{f}\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}c\int xf^{2}(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}. $$

Finally, $\mathcal{E}_{f}^{\mathrm{est}}(\bm{X},\bm{y})\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}0$ by the same concentration argument used in Section B.2. This concludes the proof. ∎

## Appendix I Decentralized Learning - Proof of Theorem 3.9

### I.1 Notation and The Bias–Variance Decomposition

We begin by rewriting the aggregated estimator in a form that absorbs the aggregation weights into the shrinkage functions themselves, which makes the subsequent bias–variance decomposition more transparent. Throughout, the index $\ell$ refers to a client and ranges over $\{1,\dots,K\}$ , the index $j$ refers to a spike and ranges over $\{1,\dots,s\}$ , and the index $i$ refers to an eigenvector and ranges over $\{1,\dots,p\}$ . For each client $\ell$ , the corresponding spectral shrinkage estimator is

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\ell}=f_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{y}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}}={\bm{W}}_{\ell}f_{\ell}({\bm{\Lambda}}_{\ell})\bm{W}_{\ell}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{y}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}},\qquad\text{where }\quad\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}=\bm{W}_{\ell}{\bm{\Lambda}}_{\ell}\bm{W}_{\ell}^{\top}. $$

The next proposition rewrites each local estimator in a form that separates signal and noise, and then introduces a rescaled spectral shrinkage function that incorporates the aggregation weight.

#### Lemma I.1.

For each client $\ell$ , define

$$ \widetilde{f}_{\ell}(x):=K\rho_{\ell}f_{\ell}(x),\qquad\widetilde{\bm{\beta}}_{\ell}:=\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{y}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}}. $$

Moreover, if we let $g_{\ell}(x):=x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(x)-1$ , then

$$ \widetilde{\bm{\beta}}_{\ell}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}=g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}){\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}}, $$

and hence

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{agg}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}(\widetilde{\bm{\beta}}_{\ell}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0})=.\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}){\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}}\,. $$

Lemma I.1 is useful because it expresses the aggregated estimator as an average of $K$ terms with the same normalization. This allows the conditional prediction risk to be decomposed into a bias term and $K$ separate variance contributions. The proof is a straightforward algebraic manipulation and follows the first part of Section B.2. We omit the details. Using these notations, we can deduce a standard bias–variance decomposition of the prediction risk of the aggregate estimator.

#### Lemma I.2.

The following decomposition holds:

$$ \|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{agg}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}=\|\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{agg}}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\mathcal{V}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{agg}}+\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{agg}}, $$

where the bias term is

$$ \mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{agg}}:=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}){\bm{\beta}}_{0}, $$

the variance contribution of client $\ell$ is

$$ \mathcal{V}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{agg}}:=\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{K^{2}n_{\ell}}{\sf tr}\bigl(\bm{\Sigma}\,\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}\,{\widetilde{f}_{\ell}}^{2}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\bigr), $$

and $\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{agg}}\xrightarrow{a.s.}0$ as $p\to\infty$ .

In the next lemma, we rewrite the conditional bias norm in a form that separates the bulk contribution from the spike contributions.

#### Lemma I.3.

We can decompose $\|\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{agg}}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}$ as

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}){\bm{\beta}}_{0}\right\|^{2}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}} \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{K^{2}}\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\right)^{2}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\frac{1}{K^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\,\left({\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\bm{v}_{j}\right)^{2} \displaystyle:=\mathcal{B}_{0}^{\mathrm{agg}}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\mathcal{B}_{j}^{\mathrm{agg}}. $$

Here $\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{agg}}_{0}$ corresponds to the contribution from the isotropic part of ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ , while each $\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{agg}}_{j}$ captures the contribution of the spike direction $\bm{v}_{j}$ . It is immediate from Lemma I.2 and Lemma I.3 that to quantify the limiting prediction risk, we need to establish the limit of the bulk bias term $\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{agg}}_{0}$ , the spike bias terms $\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{agg}}_{j}$ , and the client-specific variance terms $\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{agg}}_{\ell}$ .

### I.2 Proof of Theorem 3.9

From the definition of $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}_{K}(\rho_{1},\cdots,\rho_{k},f_{1},\dots,f_{K})$ (Equation (3.7)) and the definition of $(\tilde{f}_{1},\dots,\tilde{f}_{k})$ and $\hat{\bm{\beta}}_{\rm agg}$ (Lemma B.1), we have:

$$ \mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}_{K}(\rho_{1},\cdots,\rho_{k},f_{1},\dots,f_{K})=\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}_{K}(\widetilde{f}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{f}_{K}):=\lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\to\infty\end{subarray}}\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{agg}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2} $$

First, we argue that the limit exists almost surely. Towards that end, we use the same tools as used in Section B and in the proof of Theorem 3.10. In particular, using the Radon–Nikodym identities from Lemma A.14 and the functions introduced in (B.1), we obtain the following:

#### Lemma I.4.

For any functions $f_{1},\dots,f_{K}\in\mathcal{F}$ and $\rho_{1},\dots,\rho_{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}$ , the almost sure limiting prediction risk of $\widehat{{\bm{\beta}}}_{\mathrm{agg}}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}_{K}(\widetilde{f}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{f}_{K}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\|\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\|_{w}^{2}-2K\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle g,\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\rangle_{w}+2\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\langle h_{0},\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\langle h_{0},\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w} \displaystyle+2\sum_{j=1}^{s}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\alpha_{j}^{2}\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\langle h_{j},\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\langle h_{j},\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle h_{j},\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\right)^{2}+K^{2}\left(r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\right). $$

To obtain the optimal shrinkage rule for each client, we minimize the limiting risk with respect to $(\tilde{f}_{1},\dots,\tilde{f}_{K})$ . We first show that at the minimum value, all shrinkage rules $\widetilde{f}_{\ell}$ are equal to each other, which essentially proves the second part of Theorem 3.9. To do this, we introduce the mean and the centered functions

$$ \bar{\vartheta}:=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\widetilde{f}_{\ell},\qquad\vartheta_{\ell}:=\widetilde{f}_{\ell}-\bar{\vartheta}\,. $$

It is immediate that $\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\vartheta_{\ell}=0$ . By some simple algebraic manipulation, we can rewrite the limiting risk, obtained in Lemma I.4, as follows:

#### Lemma I.5.

Under the assumptions of Lemma I.4,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}_{K}(\widetilde{f}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{f}_{K}) \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{a.s.}}}{{=}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\|\vartheta_{\ell}\|_{w}^{2}-\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle h_{0},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}^{2}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}^{2} \displaystyle\quad+K\|\bar{\vartheta}\|_{w}^{2}-2K^{2}\langle g,\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\,K(K-1)\langle h_{0},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2} \displaystyle\quad+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\alpha_{j}^{2}\bigl(K(K-1)\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{j}K^{2}\bigr)\langle h_{j},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2}+K^{2}\left(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\right). $$

Crucially, note that in the form above the mean and the centered functions decouple so we can minimize them separately. Indeed, the next Lemma shows that the term that depends on $\bar{\vartheta}$ is always nonnegative. This is the key step forcing all optimal functions $\widetilde{f}_{\ell}$ to coincide on $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}\setminus\{0\}$ .

#### Lemma I.6.

For every $\phi\in\mathcal{F}$ ,

$$ \|\phi\|_{w}^{2}-\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\langle h_{0},\phi\rangle_{w}^{2}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\langle h_{j},\phi\rangle_{w}^{2}\geq 0. $$

Moreover, equality holds if and only if $\phi$ vanishes on $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}\setminus\{0\}$ .

Now we have all the tools required to prove Theorem 3.9.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.9.

From Lemma I.5, we know that optimizing $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}_{K}(\widetilde{f}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{f}_{K})$ is equivalent to optimizing the prediction risk as a function of $(\vartheta_{1},\dots,\vartheta_{k},\bar{v})$ . By Lemma I.6, we can conclude that any optimizer must have

$$ \vartheta_{\ast,1}(x)=\vartheta_{\ast,2}(x)=\dots=\vartheta_{\ast,K}(x)=0,\qquad\qquad\text{for }x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}\setminus\{0\}. $$

Thus, it is enough to minimize

$$ \displaystyle K\|\bar{\vartheta}\|_{w}^{2}-2K^{2}\langle g,\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\,K(K-1)\langle h_{0},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2} \displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\bigl(K(K-1)\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{j}K^{2}\bigr)\langle h_{j},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2}+K^{2}\left(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\right), $$

or equivalently, after dropping terms that do not depend on $\bar{\vartheta}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}_{K}(\bar{\vartheta}):=\|\bar{\vartheta}\|_{w}^{2}-2K\langle g,\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\,(K-1)\langle h_{0},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\bigl((K-1)\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{j}K\bigr)\langle h_{j},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2}. $$

As in Lemma B.2, we can characterize the minimizer using a linear operator. Define $\mathcal{A}_{K}:\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{F}$ as

$$ \mathcal{A}_{K}f=f+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}(K-1)\,\langle f,h_{0}\rangle_{w}\,h_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\left((K-1)\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+K\delta_{j}\right)\,\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\langle f,h_{j}\rangle_{w}\,h_{j}. $$

For one client $K=1$ , the operator $\mathcal{A}_{K}$ simplies to $\mathcal{A}_{1}=\mathcal{A}$ where $\mathcal{A}$ is the operator introduced in Lemma B.2. It is straightforward to check that $\mathcal{A}_{K}$ satisfies the same properties as $\mathcal{A}$ ; in particular, $\mathcal{A}_{K}$ is positive-semidefinite, self-adjoint and

$$ \mathcal{R}^{\text{avg}}(\bar{\vartheta})=\langle\mathcal{A}_{K}\,\bar{\vartheta},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}-2K\langle g,\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}. $$

Next, we prove that there exists $f_{K}^{\ast}\in\mathcal{F}$ such that $[\mathcal{A}_{K}f_{K}^{\ast}](x)=g(x)$ for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ . As in Section B.3, we consider a candidate

$$ f_{K}^{\ast}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{s}b^{(K)}_{j}h_{j}(x) $$

and find real coefficients $\{b^{(K)}_{0},b^{(K)}_{1},\dots,b^{(K)}_{s}\}$ for which

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{K}f_{K}^{\ast} \displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{s}b^{(K)}_{i}h_{i}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}(K-1)\left(\sum_{i=0}^{s}b^{(K)}_{i}\langle h_{i},h_{0}\rangle_{w}\right)h_{0} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\bigl((K-1)\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+K\delta_{j}\bigr)\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\sum_{i=0}^{s}b^{(K)}_{i}\langle h_{i},h_{j}\rangle_{w}\right)h_{j} $$

is exactly equal to $g(x)$ . Equivalently, recall $\bm{H}$ from Section B.3 and define
